rationale: Anytime Mailbox is a SaaS virtual-mailbox service with public docs and a help center, so publishing llms.txt or agent-oriented docs is a fair question and the axis applies. A direct probe of /llms.txt returned HTTP 404. No evidence shows any agent-oriented documentation; the cited pages are consumer marketing and help-center articles.

A virtual mailbox service holds user data (scanned mail, packages, calls), so it could plausibly ship AI-generated insights or suggestions, and the axis applies. The evidence covers only manual mail handling: viewing scans, forwarding, shredding, check deposit, and team access. Nothing documents AI-generated insights, summaries, or suggestions inside the product.

Background automation, such as auto-scan or auto-forward rules, is a plausible capability for a virtual mailbox service, so the axis applies. However, the evidence only describes manual, on-demand requests ('with a few taps, you can request that the operator open and scan...') and one-off pickup scheduling. Nothing in the pack shows rules or automations that run autonomously, and the probes found no API or OpenAPI surface.

A built-in AI assistant is a plausible feature for a virtual mailbox SaaS, so the axis applies. However, the evidence pack never mentions an AI assistant or agent. The task requests it does describe (scan, forward, shred) are fulfilled by human mail-center operators, which is an adjacent feature and earns no credit.

Headless or programmatic automation is a fair question for a virtual-mailbox SaaS, since such a service could expose an API or CLI, so the axis applies. The evidence only describes management through a phone app or web portal, and probes found no OpenAPI spec or llms.txt. Nothing shows the product can run headlessly or in CI.

Anytime Mailbox is a virtual mailbox and mail-handling service. Acting as an MCP client that plugs in external MCP servers and calls their tools is an AI-agent/assistant role, which is a category error for this kind of product. Nothing in the evidence shows it ships any agent or MCP-client capability that would make the axis apply.

Anytime Mailbox is a SaaS virtual mailbox service, so an official MCP server is a plausible capability and the axis applies. The evidence pack contains no mention of an MCP server or any agent-facing interface, and the probes for llms.txt and OpenAPI specs all returned 404.

A virtual mailbox SaaS could plausibly offer a natural-language or AI-assistant interface, so this axis applies. The evidence only describes operating the service through taps in a phone app or web portal (open/scan, forward, shred, schedule pickup). There is nothing on natural-language commands or a conversational interface, and the llms.txt and OpenAPI probes both returned 404, so no AI-facing surface was found.

Anytime Mailbox is a virtual mailbox SaaS, and such a service could plausibly ship an official CLI, so the axis applies. The evidence only documents mail management through a phone app and web portal, with no mention of any CLI. Probes also found no llms.txt or OpenAPI spec.

A virtual mailbox SaaS could plausibly offer a public API, so the axis applies. The evidence only shows the service being managed through a phone app and web portal. Probes found no OpenAPI spec and no llms.txt (all candidate paths returned 404), and nothing documents a public API.

Anytime Mailbox is a virtual mailbox SaaS that could plausibly offer an API with scoped credentials, so the axis applies. The evidence pack documents no API keys, tokens, or permission scopes.
